title: Anticipating and rapidly responding to respiratory virus outbreaks with continuous air sampling in K-12 schools
text:
We have shown that air samplers in schools detect respiratory viruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and in-
fluenza viruses. This project will deploy air samplers to 16 K-12 schools to explore whether air sampling
accurately assesses SARS-CoV-2 and influenza virus risk in schools and forecasts transmission of these
viruses in the communities where the schools are located. Viral sequencing of air samples will also be
performed to ascertain which viral variants are circulating and spreading within and between schools
and the broader community.

title: New tools for quantitative non-invasive recording of biochemical signals
text:
In this project, a new class of biological reporters will be developed and deployed to identify key bottlenecks in
the translation of CAR chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, an emerging therapeutic approach to
cancer treatment. This work will reveal new avenues to improve the overall general performance and durability
of CAR T cells, by enabling researchers to easily view the history of calcium signaling in these cells. The imaging
probes leverage state-of-the-art bioluminescent and fluorescent proteins, which naturally emit and transform
light, to build probes that non-invasively record biochemical activities in living cells.

title: Development of a CRISPR-Cas13 Gene Therapy for SOD1-Linked ALS
text:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating and fatal disorder with no cure and few effective treatment
options. We will develop a gene therapy for ALS by engineering an RNA-targeting CRISPR-based technology to
silence the production of mutant forms of superoxide dismutase 1, a protein responsible for ~20% of all inherited
cases of ALS. Thus, by harnessing an innovative technology for transcriptional engineering that can overcome
the limitations of traditional methods for gene silencing, we will develop a new, permanently effective therapy for
SOD1-linked familial ALS.

title: The Genetic and Epigenetic Mechanisms of Phenotypic Innovation
text:
The regulation of transcription in humans has a significant impact on many aspects of health and disease, but
the effects on phenotypes are not fully understood, especially in the context of new genes and their functional
innovation. We propose to use fruit flies as a model to investigate the extent of gene expression variation and
the role of transcription factors in the evolution of new genes and new expression. The findings of this research
will be valuable in our understanding of transcription-associated disorders such as Li-Fraumeni syndrome and
verbal dyspraxia, as well as the regulatory mechanisms underlying sperm fertility.

title: Integration of biophysics and deep learning to understand species-specificity of fertilization and the rapid evolution of protein disorder
text:
A paradigm of molecular evolution and biophysics is that proteins adopt regular three-dimensional
shapes necessary for their cellular functions, yet recent studies of intrinsically disordered proteins support that
protein dynamics contribute to both functional plasticity and evolvability over millions of years. The goals of this
R35 MIRA are to integrate high throughput mutagenesis screens with biophysical assays and the development
of new deep learning models to understand how rapid evolution shapes molecular dynamics and interfaces.
These questions will be explored using species-specificity of fertilization as a model.

title: MOSAIC: Biospecimen Core
text:
BIOSPECIMEN CORE 
The Biospecimen Core will assist the Center through two specific aims: Aim 1) collect and store biopsies, Aim 
2) run initial tissue characterization of immunohistochemistry and sequencing. The duties of the Biospecimen 
Core Mayo Clinic Arizona (MCA) and Columbia University Medical Center (CUMC) and will support both projects. 
The data generated by the Biospecimen Core will be transferred to the Data Integration and Computation Core, 
where it will be stored, further processed including batch correction and atlas alignment, and integrated into 
computational modeling tools.

title: Vision Sciences Training Grant
text:
The goal of the proposed program is to support predoctoral students in vision research - to expand their
understanding of current basic and clinical investigations on the eye and visual pathways, and to provide
professional development in academic and science-allied careers. Areas of program strength include studies
of higher-level influences on visual perception, of development and plasticity of visual circuitry, and of genetics
and cell biology of retinal degeneration. This training is critical to the next generation of scientists who will
tackle perturbations of vision at these levels.

title: Molecular Architecture of the Vaccinia virus factory
text:
Human poxvirus outbreaks can rapidly challenge global human health, and human
monkeypox (Mpox) with significant case fatality rates has the potential to become
established in the human population. Using Vaccinia virus (the Mpox vaccine), this grant
proposes a new approach to detecting protein interfaces that form during the natural
assembly of new viruses inside the infected cell. Such interfaces comprise perhaps the
most target rich environment for future novel drugs.

title: Control of Virulence Properties in the Major Human Oral Fungal Pathogen Candida albicans by the Asc1 Translational Regulator
text:
Relevance to public health: Candida albicans is a major human oral fungal pathogen that shows increasing
resistance to antifungal treatment. Translational regulation of C. albicans virulence properties remains an
unexplored and unexploited avenue for antifungal drug development. This project will determine how the Asc1
translational regulator controls C. albicans host environmental stress responses, morphogenesis, and other
virulence-related processes in order to provide information leading to the development of new and more
effective antifungals for the treatment of oral candidiasis.

title: Malaria and Mosquito/Tick-borne Diseases
text:
This Malaria and Mosquito/Tick-borne Diseases training program for 3 doctoral students and 2 postdoctoral
fellows is highly relevant to national interests in vector-borne infectious diseases. The program will train
students broadly in the molecular aspects of malaria and mosquito arboviral biology and pathogenesis, as well
as in the ecology and epidemiology of mosquito/tick-borne pathogens and the role of mosquito vectors in
transmission. The public health relevance derives from not only the mosquito disease specific knowledge
(Dengue and Zika as well as malaria), but also general scientific concepts in critical thinking focused on Rigor,
Reproducibility and Responsibility (R3).

title: Targeted ColQ gene therapy for Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes
text:
ColQ CMS is a rare neuromuscular disorder with no cure associated. Severe limb-girdle pattern of weakness,
choking spells, respiratory insufficiency, severe scoliosis present early on during the disease progression
with early death not uncommon among these patients. This project aims to validate the safety and efficacy
of a new gene therapy product for ColQ CMS able to transform clinical practice from chronic administration
of drugs to alleviate symptoms to a one-off, non-pharmacological treatment, administered through a single
intravenous injection. The project is expected to unveil important insights on the mechanism of action of
Neuromuscular Junction as well to explore the existence of a shared gene therapy development pathway for
CMS.

title: Imaging Mass Spectrometry-Based Metabolomic Analysis of the Alzheimer's Brain
text:
This study will provide a comprehensive metabolomic landscape on the cell-type specific metabolomic
changes during aging and the process of neurodegeneration when the brain is exposed to pathologic amyloid
β and pathologic tau. This information will provide opportunities to develop new AD treatments targeting
microglia and astrocytes.

title: Mechanisms of Stem Cell Regulation during Tissue Renewal and Cancer Development
text:
This proposal embodies a multiscale approach to define biological mechanisms underlying the survival and
proliferation of cells with DNA damage during tissue renewal, which is critical to a wide range of human clinical
problems, including cancer and aging. Our analysis considers cellular decisions in situ as tissues undergo
renewal in the complexity of the adult body. Uniquely, we evaluate the development of the most pervasive
cancer features in only 12 days and neural signals that can reverse the cancer phenotype.

title: DNA-Protein Cross-Linking Sequencing for Genome-Wide Mapping of Abasic Sites at Single-Nucleotide Resolution
text:
Endogenous metabolism and environmental exposure can produce numerous DNA lesions, which may lead to
accelerated aging, cancer, and neurodegenerative disorders. In this proposal, we will establish an innovative
and powerful method for exploring how the induction and repair of abasic sites are influenced by toxicant
exposure and epigenetic state of chromatin. The outcome of the proposed work will enhance our understanding
about the contributions of environmental exposure- and endogenous metabolism-induced abasic sites in the
etiology of human diseases, which will ultimately lead to better strategies for the prevention and therapeutic
interventions of human cancer and aging-related diseases.

title: Amplification-free detection of specific Leishmania species using CRISPR-Cas12
text:
Leishmaniasis, a neglected tropical disease with widespread impact caused by multiple protozoan species,
requires accurate species-level identification for effective treatment and improved patient outcomes. However,
few diagnostic tools are available in resource-limited settings for species-specific epidemiological monitoring
and control of leishmaniasis. This study proposes to apply CRISPR-Cas12 direct detection technology to
develop a simplified and rapid method for detecting species-specific DNA sequences, improving the
accessibility of critical diagnostics for this complex disease.

title: Extracellular vesicles as nanotheranostic platform in neuroinflammation
text: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are the most widely used type of cells in stem cell therapy, with over 1,000 registered clinical trials primarily focused on immunosuppression of inflammatory disease. “MSCs” are often termed “medicinal stem cells”, as they secrete multiple beneficial factors in the form of extracellular vesicles (EVs) that have trophic homing properties for sites of inflammation. However, the use of MSCs is limited by complex regulatory issues and logistics, low cell viability, and high costs. The field of cell therapy has now been shifting to the production of EVs as a “cell-free” alternative. Similar to tracking whole cells, it will be imperative to be able to track the biodistribution of these therapeutic EVs in vivo in order to interpret and improve therapeutic outcome. We propose to develop two types of labeled MSC-derived EV formulations and will compare their in vivo imaging (MRI and MPI) and therapeutic properties to unmodified, naïve EVs, that we hypothesize may still be trackable with CEST MRI by virtue of their mannose-rich membrane composition. Based upon the existing clinical trials using MSCs in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), we will evaluate our MSC-EV formulations in vivo using an experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) MS mouse model and a superoxide dismutase-decificient transgenic ALS mouse model. To this end, we propose the following specific aims: AIM 1: To develop magnetically labeled MSC-EVs as a bimodal negative MRI contrast agent and magnetic particle imaging (MPI) tracer. We will use electroporation to load EVs with superparamagnetic iron oxides (SPIOs). Unlike with MRI, the number of MSC- SPIO-EVs can be quantified with MPI. AIM 2: To develop gadolinium-labeled MSC-EVs as positive MRI contrast agent. We will use lipophilic gadolinium chelates and lipid insertion techniques to render EVs with paramagnetic membranes. AIM 3: To develop unlabeled MSC-EVs as diaCEST MRI contrast agent. We will take advantage of the natural expression of high-mannose type N glycans on EV membranes which provide contrast on mannose-weighted CEST MRI, without the need of further vesicle manipulation. AIM 4: To track the in vivo distribution and therapeutic outcome of labeled and unlabeled EVs in a mouse models of EAE and ALS. This will serve as an internal JHU validation study. We will investigate various administration routes and use standard behavioral scoring tests to correlate the diagnostic and therapeutic outcome measures of our nanotheranostic approach. We will compare and validate all three MSC-EV imaging strategies in terms of sensitivity, specificity, and EV functionality. Upon proper synthesis, characterization, and in vivo validation, we will disseminate our SPIO-MSC-EVs, Gd-MSC-EVs, and unlabeled EVs to the CPS, SPs, and beyond.

title: Development of a Novel, Safe, Easily Standardized, and Cost-Effective Cell Growth Supplement for Diverse Cell Culture Applications
text:
In cell culture, growth supplements provide essential nutrients, growth factors, and hormones critical for
supporting cell health and proliferation, making them indispensable in biotechnology and medicine. However,
widely used supplements like FBS and hPL have significant drawbacks, including issues with safety,
standardization, cost, scalability, and ethical concerns. Our recent preliminary data demonstrate that a novel
supplement, hMPL, derived from an immortal cancer cell line, addresses many of these limitations while
supporting robust MSC proliferation and growth. This Phase I proposal aims to test hMPL’s mitogenic activity
compared to FBS and hPL, paving the way for Phase II studies on large-scale production and broader stem
cell applications. The ultimate goal is to develop a novel, safe, easily standardized, and cost-effective cell
growth supplement for diverse cell culture applications.

title: Controlling the Niche to Control Clonal Hematopoiesis
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because identification of the mechanisms by which clonal
hematopoiesis (CH) evolves is relevant to virtually all persons over the age of 50 years who harbor CH mutated
stem cells and is also relevant to efforts to limit the cardiovascular complications of CH. This work is consistent
with the NIH goal of fostering innovative research strategies for improving health, and with the NHLBI mission
of supporting research that promotes the prevention and treatment of blood diseases, in this case, the
currently non-modifiable risk from CH for adverse events and death. This work is also consistent with the NCI
mission of supporting research to advance the treatment of cancer and the studies are responsive to the PA in
presenting a discrete, specified, circumscribed project in an area of the investigators' specific interests and
competencies, based on the mission of the NIH to enable the translation of basic discoveries into clinical
practice research.

title: Illuminating the secretome: a protein tagging resource
text:
Secreted proteins play an important role in development and aging and numerous human
diseases have been linked to aberrant function of secreted proteins. Yet where these proteins
are expressed and localized is poorly understood. We will create the first resource of genetic
stocks expressing fluorescently tagged secretome proteins using a highly tractable model
organism, the nematode C. elegans which will provide broad insight into the function of
conserved, secreted proteins.

title: Treating Non-Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer Using the Sodium/Iodide Symporter to Deliver Targeted Internal Radiation Therapy along with Intravesical Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor and Oncolytic Reovirus
text:
The goal of this research project is to develop novel treatments for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
(NMIBC), a common and dangerous cancer that often comes back after being treated, and for which current
treatments are inadequate. Specifically, we will determine the effects of combining three different types of
treatments that are delivered directly to the bladder: 1) oncolytic reoviruses, a type of virus that prefers to infect
cancer cells and makes them more likely to be killed by the immune system; 2) immune checkpoint inhibitors,
drugs that block defensive proteins (called checkpoints) produced by cancer cells; and 3) targeted internal
radiation therapy (TIRT), in which we administer radioactive agents, such as radioiodide, that are specifically
brought into the cancer cells by a specialized protein we introduce—the sodium/iodide symporter (NIS)—and kill
the cancer cells from the inside. Developing new and effective combination therapies for NMIBC in this way could
significantly improve outcomes for patients suffering from this type of cancer, and put us in an excellent position
to design future clinical trials for these anticancer therapies.
